content:
I just want to contribute a voice in this thread on record, that there are still users who strongly prefer λ over fun for lambda notation. These are my thoughts based on my own experience in the language, coming from a background of a programmer using Lean for functional programming: Happy to hear any counter-points or corrections if i'm missing considerations from prior discussions.

  • I write anonymous functions a massive amount of times more than the amount of scenarios where I might want to use λ as a term name. A better notation for something I use all the time is worth the occasional workarounds in naming variables.
  • λ is better for readability:
    • it is 1 character long, which means easy visual parsing, and helps keep expressions on a single-line, where 3 characters is sometimes just a bit too much in dense expressions.
    • It is universally known by functional programmers as the notation for lambda calculus, which this language is based on and anyone learning the language will encounter anyway and should be expected to get familiar with given dependent typing theory.
    • fun is english phoneme, which means that my brain cannot help but audibly sound out the word "fun" when read, which is awkward, whereas with λ I just see that as "the symbol for functions" and read along without interruption.
    • it goes better with the rest of Lean's coding style ethos and aesthetic. We don't write forall, we write ∀. I think it would be ironic for Lean to be one of the only FP languages that goes all-in on embracing symbols everywhere, only to not use the canonical symbol for the most foundational construct in the language theory, instead staying with the more mainstream fun keyword. In those more mainstream languages that use fun, like F#, users even complain about the look, and request support for λ or some other terse alternative (which is shot down due to anti-symbol sentiment usually). It would be ironic for the real lambda notation to still not have a home in Lean of all languages.

At the very least, if we are considering introducing breaking changes to the language, we should also consider a more terse alternative to fun to replace it with, like having ↦ be enough for parsing e.g. x ↦ x*2 instead of λ x ↦ x *2 - though I still don't like the idea of deprecating λ in the core language.

Marvin said:

  • fun is english phoneme, which is awkward

So should we get rid of def as well? :upside_down:

Marvin said:

more terse alternative to fun to replace it with, like having ↦ be enough for parsing e.g. x ↦ x*2 instead of λ x ↦ x *2

(. * 2) is this terse notation
(Or with more unicode, (· * 2) :) )

Jovan Gerbscheid said:

So should we get rid of def as well? :

I do dislike def for the same reasoning. I would rather it be define, let, or some bulletpoint-esque symbol. Maybe that sounds strange to you at first, but I wager that most of us here would prefer inductive over induc and structure over struct (which are both longer than define). Too late now though.

def is much easier to accept given that 1) it's just the toplevel-keyword, and 2) what else would we go with? There are not many other good options.

With lambdas, 1) it's more important that they remain elegant as they are used deeply all throughout expressions. It's more important for expressions to look nice than for keywords. And 2) it is obvious what better choice exists for conveying lambdas: the lambda symbol! It's what you would expect to be the notation, so much so that languages like Haskell try to imitate it with ASCII.

Eric Wieser said:

Marvin said:

more terse alternative to fun to replace it with, like having ↦ be enough for parsing e.g. x ↦ x*2 instead of λ x ↦ x *2

(. * 2) is this terse notation

This has very limited use case since you can only refer to a particular parameter once, and sometimes you do want to name things. I agree point-free is the most terse, I prefer using it when I can. I am only saying that fun is an irritation to see and read. If we were to deprecate lambda notation, we could deprecate this notation as well.

Marvin said:

With lambdas, 1) it's more important that they remain elegant as they are used deeply all throughout expressions. It's more important for expressions to look nice than for keywords. And 2) it is obvious what better choice exists for conveying lambdas: the lambda symbol! It's what you would expect to be the notation, so much so that languages like Haskell try to imitate it with ASCII.

This very much depends on your background. There are swaths of mathematicians for which λ\lambdaλ has many different meanings (like scalar in a field), and who have never seen it used in lambda expressions before. (Of course they have seen expressions like (x↦x2)(x \mapsto x^2)(x↦x2) many times in their life. They get by without needing λ\lambdaλ for that.)

Yeah, but I would think if that learning and becoming proficient in a dependently typed functional programming language like Lean4 definitionally means making this area of computer science part of your background, familiarizing yourself with the tradition and material. Is Lean4 not inherently a 'computer science phenomenon'?

This next part is not rhetorical, I would like someone to clear my confusion if they know - it is genuinely not clear to me:
1) to what extent Lean4 the language and Mathlib are the same project.
2} who the target audience for the language is. Mathematicians? Computer scientists? Functional programmers? I assumed it is the intersection of those three, rather than just the first group.

The website and documentation does advertise Lean not only as a theorem prover for mathematicians but also as a serious functional programming language with dependent typing, and that is what brought me here.

Lean 4 is a programming language. Mathlib is some code written in that language. Many users of mathlib such as myself know only a small fragment of the programming language and in practice never write lambdas or do anything programmy like that -- I just prove theorems stated using typically very complex structures, and make more structures.
The target of the language is more like the union of the three, not the intersection. What you are observing is simply that it's hard to please all of the people all of the time
I would add to that union: software engineers, scientists interested in mathematical modeling, AI researchers and engineers, hobbyists, and other interested people.
The corollary of this diversity is that it’s much nicer if blocking λ for that weird function definition notation is fully opt-in and not the default behavior.

Marvin said:

Yeah, but I would think if that learning and becoming proficient in a dependently typed functional programming language like Lean4 definitionally means making this area of computer science part of your background, familiarizing yourself with the tradition and material. Is Lean4 not inherently a 'computer science phenomenon'?

Reality simply does not agree with you. The good news is that you can definitely use Lean the way you want to use it.

And if λ is ever removed from the core language, Lean is flexible enough that you can add it back in yourself!

(Idle thought: there's something mildly amusing about how people can have very particular preferences about the abstraction operator ;-) )
Yes this is part of the good news I was mentioning.

I think the biggest difference that removing the special handling for λ would bring is that λx (no spaces) is currently parsed as two tokens, λ and x, and would otherwise be parsed as one (the identifier λx). Perhaps it makes sense to warn on having λx without a space so that we can eventually make λ an identifier character (and similarly for Σx).

Kyle Miller said:

(Idle thought: there's something mildly amusing about how people can have very particular preferences about the abstraction operator ;-) )

It is less important to me that we pay homage to the traditional lambda notation and more important that a construct I use all of the time, is not clunky to read and look at. λ happens to look great. If some other notation were proposed besides fun, I would be open to that as well.

And if λ is ever removed from the core language, Lean is flexible enough that you can add it back in yourself!

That's good to hear. Is the other direction possible? An opt-out setting, where λ is enabled by default, and you can disable it per file or per project to allow naming identifiers λ? I think that would be the most accommodating option, there will likely be far more people who use anonymous functions daily than who are working on a formalizing a topic where λ is used to mean something else.

Marvin said:

If some other notation were proposed besides fun, I would be open to that as well.

Well for completeness, did you know you could also have no fun:

example : False → Nat := nofun

and zero fun with Mathlib:

import Mathlib
noncomputable example : ℕ →₀ ℕ := fun₀ | 1 => 2

Marvin said:

With lambdas, 1) it's more important that they remain elegant as they are used deeply all throughout expressions. It's more important for expressions to look nice than for keywords. And 2) it is obvious what better choice exists for conveying lambdas: the lambda symbol! It's what you would expect to be the notation, so much so that languages like Haskell try to imitate it with ASCII.

Please let us never use \x => for fun x => or λ x => or whatever!

Marvin said:

That's good to hear. Is the other direction possible? An opt-out setting, where λ is enabled by default, and you can disable it per file or per project to allow naming identifiers λ? I think that would be the most accommodating option, there will likely be far more people who use anonymous functions daily than who are working on a formalizing a topic where λ is used to mean something else.

I think you have an extremely wrong idea of who is currently using Lean and what they do with it.
Or maybe just an extremely wrong idea about how much λ\lambdaλ comes up as a variable in linear algebra :-)
I think the different opinions are clear. Removing it as default notation, but allowing it to be enabled again by e.g. open scoped LambdaFun should hopefully satisfy everyone.

Patrick Massot said:

I think you have an extremely wrong idea of who is currently using Lean and what they do with it.

I am sure the majority of users are currently using it for writing math formalizations that are not meant to be ran. I do also see functional programmers on the discords, reddit, etc. who are exploring and successfully using the language for general applications. That number only rises as time goes on. Is there any data on this?

A couple months ago we had a mainstream coding YouTuber post a video about Lean that reached over 100k viewers. I hear there are people working on proper web server libraries, WASM support, and so on.

Anyway, I am thinking about Lean's longterm potential. It is clearly a cutting edge, feature rich programming language with fantastic tooling, that can compete with similar industry-aspiring languages like F* and Idris. The major drawback that Lean has compared to mainstream languages like Haskell, Scala, etc is the absence of libraries, and that is improving every day.

There is an impression some have that if a language is built for theorem proving, that somehow implies that it is cannot be a good choice for general purpose industry programming. I think that assumption is very wrong. Having a sophisticated type system is beneficial to building and maintaining applications, and I see a future where these next generation functional languages become realistic options for skillful programmers in everyday programming.

Floris van Doorn said:

Removing it as default notation, but allowing it to be enabled again by e.g. open scoped LambdaFun should hopefully satisfy everyone.

I assume that this means we would have to write open scoped LambdaFun in every single file in every project forever? The number of people willing to do that will be extremely small, even among those who like the notation, meaning this would become an idiosyncratic style used only by myself, and all community projects would ban it in their style guide and all newcomers would be advised not to use it. I'm not satisfied with that.

If a way to enable the notation codebase-wide were provided, then that is a much less alienating proposal that could satisfy everyone. Otherwise, it is really just proposing that the notation go extinct.

In your own project you can definitely enable the notation globally, without having to write anything like open scoped in every file. Just declare a global macro.
If you ask that it should be globally enabled in Lean Core/Mathlib, then we might have irreconcilable different in desires. For one, because it is currently hard/impossible to disable global macros.

I do also see functional programmers on the discords, reddit, etc. who are exploring and successfully using the language for general applications. That number only rises as time goes on.

But do they prefer λ?

I think the different opinions are clear. Removing it as default notation, but allowing it to be enabled again by e.g. open scoped LambdaFun should hopefully satisfy everyone.

I think set_option is better since it can be easily a project-wise setting by writing it in lakefile.toml.

I agree that set_option would be better but options (currently) can't affect the token table (or more generally, the environment) and I'm not sure they should be able to. Perhaps a better alternative would be to allow project-wide opens.

Robin Arnez said:

Perhaps a better alternative would be to allow project-wide opens.

I agree, but is it not common for projects to have some "commons" file, like Mathlib's Mathlib.Init, that every file imports? This is similar in spirit to what some other languages do, such as CSS resets, TypeScript's global.d.ts, LaTeX's preamble, Python's __init__.py

Oh actually I now realize that importing a file doesn't inherit what it opens, hmm, well maybe that could be a feature
This discussion looks like it might actually be converging into an RFC!

Just for the completeness of this discussion (which took ~36500 characters) you can enable the notation with this command (just 64 characters)

import Lean

open Lean.Parser.Term

macro "β" bs:funBinder* ", " b: term : term => `(fun $bs* => $b)

-- fun x => x : ?m.704 → ?m.704
#check β x, x
-- fun x => (fun a b => b) x : (x : ?m.709) → ?m.723 x x → ?m.723 x x
#check β x, (β a b, b) x
-- fun x =>
--  match x with
--  | (x, y) => x + y : Nat × Nat → Nat
#check β ((x,y) : Nat × Nat), x+y

Just for demonstration purposes I did it with β instead of λ simulating the case when λ is treated the same as β.

Tomas Skrivan said:

(which took ~36500 characters)

Why compare the length of the macro to the length of the discussion?
To point out the somewhat pointlessness of the discussion that spiraled out a bit.

Robin Arnez said:

Perhaps a better alternative would be to allow project-wide opens.

(Note: project-/library-wide opens (or at least the underlying infrastructure), would also be useful for enabling project-/library-wide namespacing and handling the downstream impacts of such. That is, namespacing Mathlib wouldn’t be so bad if every downstream project could open Mathlib everywhere automatically. So this might be worth it for other reasons too.)

Tomas Skrivan said:

To point out the somewhat pointlessness of the discussion that spiraled out a bit.

I don't think it's very nice to call a language design discussion pointless, especially using sarcasm through character counts.

If by "spiraled" you mean "let's move the λ discussion to a separate topic" then I agree.
35 messages were moved here from #lean4 > Accept more Unicode in identifiers? by Kyle Miller.
I like the new topic name. :laughing:

Marvin said:

  • It is universally known by functional programmers as the notation for lambda calculus, which this language is based on and anyone learning the language will encounter anyway and should be expected to get familiar with given dependent typing theory.

How many programming languages actually use the unicode λ symbol for anonymous functions though? The character literally only appears once on Wikipedia's list of examples of anonymous functions in different programming languages, and that's specifically in the context of explaining that Haskell's backslash (as in \x -> x * x) is meant to visually resemble λ.

James E Hanson said:

How many programming languages actually use the unicode λ symbol for anonymous functions though?

To be fair, very few English-based programming languages use non-ASCII unicode symbols in any built-in notation, so you would expect this number to be low. Although I do agree with those who suggested that λ should be unreserved by default.

James E Hanson said:

How many programming languages actually use the unicode λ symbol for anonymous functions though?

That is due to a different reason - historically mainstream programmers have had a phobia towards the use of non-ascii symbols in code. Python literally calls their anonymous functions lambda, so the issue is clearly not familiarity with the origin of the concept. They also name their constant for π the word pi, and sqrt for √, like nearly every other language you will find on that Wikipedia list does, despite π and √ obviously being more readable.

Lean is a much newer language with a different culture, and it has demonstrated how symbols can work great in code.
tbh lambda is the thing about python I dislike the most as it's so clunky. I wish they had chosen fun as their keyword instead.

Jon Eugster said:

it's so clunky

And this is how I feel about fun. In the languages that do use fun, like F#, users complain about it's readability too.
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/1925483/f-is-the-fun-keyword-necessary
https://www.reddit.com/r/fsharp/comments/izdblx/shower_thoughtjust_for_fun_how_hard_would_it_be/
https://github.com/fsharp/fslang-suggestions/issues/634
As a mathematician by training, I find fun more readable than λ. There are different backgrounds here.
Also note that having unicode in declaration names is another issue: inputting that nicely everywhere (in emails, your chat application, ...) requires custom configuration.

Michael Rothgang said:

As a mathematician by training, I find fun more readable than λ

And do you find Sigma / DependentPair more readable than Σ? After all, Sigma types are also from this more niche computer science, type theory area of mathematics.
I'm used to Σ meaning something else (the sum sign)!

Yeah exactly, that was my familiarity too before being exposed to dependent type theory. What I'm trying to say is that I don't think we would want to discontinue the Σ notation for dependent pairs, since it's canonical in the dependent type literature, Lean4 is a dependently language, and we should expect anyone who wants to use it to become familiar with the basics of the theory. It would be strange to treat users who are familiar with lambda calculus and dependent type theory as second-class citizens in a language based on dependently typed lambda calculus.

Of course it would be great if we can enable ways to switch notation in different contexts, using Σ to mean sum for example. But the branch of mathematics that this language is based on should have priority in core notation - by using this language you are inherently operating within that branch.

And, when disagreeing about readability, we have to distinguish mere 'familiarity' from more objective metrics, like how humans visually process stuff.

If I knew the words plus, minus, but had never seen their symbols +, -, then I might initially think that the word forms are more readable, but if I would simply invest the time to find + - familiar, they would objectively become easier to parse than plus, minus ever could.

Likewise, no matter how familiar I become with the fun, it is physically longer than λ and triggers english sub-vocalization. Those facts are unchangeable, but your familiarity with λ would improve the more that you see it. (you probably would eventually prefer it over fun!)

Okay, with Tomas Skrivan's point, what about this compromise:

/--
error: Unknown identifier `λ`

Note: The global lambda notation has been disabled in version xyz, to add it back in your project, add
  macro ppAllowUngrouped "λ" x:basicFun : term => `(fun $x:basicFun)
  macro ppAllowUngrouped "λ" x:matchAltsExpr : term => `(fun $x:matchAlts)
somewhere (ideally in a file that many files import)
 -/
#guard_msgs in
def test : Nat → Nat :=
  λ n => n + 2
  • the minor thing of making basicFun and matchAltsExpr global parser aliases so you don't need import Lean.
  • maybe suggesting a concrete file that looks like a "commons" file

The compromise is incomplete if it doesn't also involve a way to enable this globally once and for-all in a codebase, not a custom prelude file that you must import into every file forever. If that is required, most users ultimately will not do it.

I think Lean really should come up with a way to set global imports / custom preluds like this at the codebase level. It would immediately solve debates like this, among others like the Mathlib namespacing issues mentioned.
Imports are already transitive. Basically every file in Mathlib has Mathlib.Init imported, without ever mentioning it.
If I'm making a library, let's say 10 files within it - none of which depend on anything else - I would have to write this lambda import in all 10 them, right?

This also sounds like I will need to mentally keep track of whether or not my lambda notation is being implicitly imported in higher-level files too, going back to reference my import lists and thinking "do any of these imports transitively import my lambda notation"? Maybe in practice this is easier than it sounds and I'm exaggerating, but it doesn't sound great.
It's probably not hard to get this working in the lakefile of your project. But I've never tried.

Johan Commelin said:

It's probably not hard to get this working in the lakefile of your project. But I've never tried.

You mean checking if an Init-like module is imported everywhere? How would this be done via lakefile?
No, I meant some option/flag/code that enables the notation.
But I've never seriously lakefiled... so I might be completely wrong.

Marvin said:

And do you find Sigma / DependentPair more readable than Σ?

The modern Lean notation is (x : α) × β x. I find it so much more readable than Σ! I think it would be reasonable to deprecate the older sigma notation given that the alternative has a lot going for it.

The problem with using a Sigma constant instead of notation isn't about whether it's a single character or not, but because Sigma (fun x : α => β x) is rather clunky.

Also, it's a bit of a "code smell" if you're overusing sigma types rather than creating a custom structure, so I don't think sigma types have much bearing here.

Too much fun can also be a bit of a code smell I think... Functional programming is about functions being values, not about avoiding naming things.

I remember back in the day learning Scheme and installing an Emacs major mode that would render lambda as λ. I found it to be very pleasing and obviously the correct thing to do. When I learned Haskell I wasn't too keen its inferior imitation, \.

However, now with about 18 years between me and then, I've realized that I probably wouldn't enable that option in the Emacs major mode today (and not just because I'm not using Scheme anymore :-) ). Syntax is important, sure, since it's the primary user interface of a programming language, but if λ vs fun had any impact on the understandability of my code, I think there must be bigger problems in the language that need solving (or more likely in my code!).

Let's look at the competing concerns:

  1. Some people want to use λ in identifiers, and λ is a common variable in math, science, engineering, and even CS (there's much more to CS than lambda calculus!)
  2. Some people want to reserve λ for lambda abstraction for aesthetics and tradition, and for advertising functional programming aspects of Lean.

Supposing there were no way to compromise (e.g. by having some global option to enable notation for a given project, without having it affect downstream projects), then I think it's hard to argue against option 1, which has the greater value to the greater Lean community.

Yes, λ is traditional, but I think part of the reason for Lean's success could be that it doesn't expect users to be "initiated into the tradition" and engage with PL or the underlying type theory. It doesn't make Lean any less of a functional programming language if you can use it without being familiar with DTT literature.

Also, if the mechanics of a language are rooted in DTT, it doesn't follow that the language ought to cater to that subcommunity. DTT is a means to an end — having a modern programming and theorem proving experience — not a research language developed to explore new DTT concepts, in which case, yeah, it would be weird if it didn't use notation that appears in the type theory literature.

Jon Eugster said:

lambda is the thing about python I dislike the most as it's so clunky

My impression is that it's meant to be a little clunky, since you're encouraged to use nested defs. It makes sense why they chose lambda at the time, but these days it can feel like a shibboleth for functional programming — at least when I explain Python's lambda to CS undergrads they find it to be rather obscure... It might even hinder learning functional programming idioms, since psychologically it doesn't help things that it starts with some obscuration.

It seems worth thinking about why it seems like a pressure point at all.

In core Lean, only two types of uses of fun really come to mind:

  1. Higher-order functions like List.map (fun x => doStuff) lst
  2. Monadic combinators like withFoo fun x => do doSomeStuff

For the first, often you see it written as lst.map fun x => doStuff, and fun serves as a kind of glorified <|.

For the second, fun ... do is sort of effectively a compound syntax.

I'm wondering what it would be like if <| had an "implicit fun". Something like this:

lst.map <| x =>
  doStuff

or this:

list.foldr (init := v) <| x acc =>
  f x acc

Relatedly, I've also wondered why couldn't <| be a prefix syntax, rather than a binary one. There are some frictions in custom notations where you can't write foo <| a b c since foo expects a term. This "implicit fun" proposal would mean that <| x y z => e could be used instead of fun expressions. (And look how nice that symmetry is with the < and the >.)

Similarly, if there were "do functions" like do x y z => doItems for fun x y z => do doItems, then one could write

lst.foldrM (init := v) do x acc =>
  doStuffWith x acc

though that's a harder sell. At least "implicit fun" means this would work:

lst.foldrM (init := v) <| x acc => do
  doStuffWith x acc

The notation doesn't just have to be for <|, but for parentheses too, thinking about <| being like an open parenthesis. For example, one might write (x y z => x + y + z).

Regarding an unrestricted x y z => x + y + z, there have been concerns about impacts on parsing — there's more to function binder syntax than just variables and type ascriptions. At least with parentheses, the problem is more localized (though still present). If there were a stronger indicator that a function was starting, like in (| x y z => x + y + z), that would be better, though I can't imagine (| actually being introduced into Lean's syntax.

Anyway, the thought is that if there's a token that often precedes fun, having fun itself be optional after such tokens might be pleasant and still reasonably clear.
iris-lean uses lambda in some places.

There's a rule that downstream users will make use of every observable feature of a language (whether or not it was intentional). Even core Lean has a few uses of λ; it's not surprising if people are using a language feature.

I went to look at iris-lean @Shreyas Srinivas, and maybe I'm missing if you mean anything by bringing up iris-lean in particular, but I don't see any meaningful use of λ. The library appears to use fun and λ interchangeably, preferring fun by a ratio of 3:1.

@Kyle Miller I don't think you engage with the main claim, which is readability, not aesthetics or tradition.

You say that you used to find lambda obviously worse than λ, which I'm sure everyone here agrees with, but then you don't explain why you no longer feel that way. Why did you find λ more pleasant? Do the advantages it had no longer apply, or do you simply not care about them anymore?

You offer a maxim about there being bigger problems to solve, but it's so unqualified that it has to be false - you don't think that the difference in keywords can have any impact on readability? Not even a small impact? And then in contradiction, you go on to speculate that lambda in Python was intentionally chosen as a clunky keyword to deter people from using it, conceding that it does have an impact.

I can post many snippets where expressions only fit neatly on my screen if I use λ instead of fun, and line-breaking would look clunky. Maybe you have a wider monitor, or maybe you're happy with reading exceedingly horizontal expressions, or maybe you turn on word-wrap that causes expressions to wrap around in unpredictable, hard-to-read ways.
When I write code, it matters a lot to me that reading experience for others will be be consistent and pleasant, so that means writing with the assumption that it looks nice on a common laptop screen with a reasonable font size, no word-wrap. That fun is an english word, sticking out in a sea of symbols, is another problem I've mentioned.

Traditional notation or advertising is not the main point. I would even be happy with 𝑓 or \ as the symbol. What matters to me is that I have a short, non-english notation, to keep readability (not understandability, not familiarity, but readability) high.

Too much fun can also be a bit of a code smell I think... Functional programming is about functions being values, not about avoiding naming things.

This is very controversial and not something we should impose onto users. What you are implying is that Agda and Haskell are inherently code-smelly languages, because they both have you define functions first by their type signature only, and only introduce names afterwards, if at all. This is something that lean supports too, e.g. f : α → β → γ := λ a b => and there are compelling arguments for this style even if it is not as popular.

I agree with you that (x : α) × β x is an equally good option for dependent pairs, my point was just to draw an analogy that keeping notation not feeling clunky is important, and the traditional theory already offers us an elegant choice, even if unfamiliar to some backgrounds.

I do think it's entirely reasonable to want to use λ as an identifier if you find that most readable for your variable, but if we grant that, then we should also grant that it is entirely reasonable to find λ most readable for your functions. I don't think it's obvious that we should prioritize the first group over the second.

For some reference, I just cmd+f searched for λ in my general-purpose app that I started on a couple weeks ago, and there is over 120 occurrences across the 16 files already. Contrast this against when Kevin said that he never writes anonymous functions. It might be hard to empathize with my position if you rarely use the construct, and is sounds like Lean-for-FP and Lean-for-Mathlib can result in very different frequencies of it's usage.
Kyle is imaging a future where you don't have to write anything at all, a parenthesis suffices. Sounds good to me.

Marvin said:

When I write code, it matters a lot to me that reading experience for others will be be consistent and pleasant

While there wasn't a poll (but see emojis here), to me it seems that most people in this thread find fun more readable than λ (or don't care). With that in mind, doesn't it mean you should strive to use fun to make it more readable for others, as you said?

If OTOH you prioritize it being readable to yourself, then what's wrong with the oneliner that enables lambda notation? If the UX of a "commons" file is bad then let's solve that instead!

I think that customizing the experience in one's own repos is a common thing across many languages and a sensible thing to do. e.g. .editorconfig, tsconfig.json, eslintrc.js, .clang-format, etc. There are even solutions to keep such files updated across all your projects, see cookiecutter.

It's clear that you feel very strongly about this lambda issue, and I find that very admirable. I also have opinions about programming syntax that I feel similarly strongly about.

Snir Broshi said:

it seems that most people in this thread find fun more readable than λ (or don't care). With that in mind, doesn't it mean you should strive to use fun to make it more readable for others, as you said?

Well as I said, I want to distinguish what's readable from what's familiar. The notation is more readable if you get used to it.

Anyway, the audience I have in mind when I write code are readers of my sort of background, the programming → mathematics pipeline, not the mathematics → programming pipeline. It sounds like most of the thread is coming from that second pipeline, though I wonder what percentage of all Lean users total it accounts for, and especially what the demographic will be in the future.

If the UX of a "commons" file is bad then let's solve that instead!

Yes, if we could get an easy way to let me globally add my own preferred notation into a project, without the chore of always needing to consider if the right imports are hooked up, I would be happy with that.

A lot of that is fair. But to respond here,

You have to make a choice here, between one use on the one hand, and virtually infinitely many uses on the other hand, so the latter is clearly more rational.

The 'one use' of denoting lambda functions is also applicable to virtually infinitely many uses, because it is a central language feature. I will use anonymous functions hundreds-to-thousands of times in some projects. Small losses in readability there will add up across all of the usages. Which of the two infinities you want to sacrifice depends on how you use the language. I understand there are many who use this language in a way that rarely involves anonymous functions, and so the current trade-off does not make sense for them. I agree we should find a way to unreserve the keyword for them, and we should find a way to make it painless to keep the notation for those who want to keep it.
